title: Labneh: What It Is, How It Is Made, and How It Differs From Greek Yogurt

seo.title: Labneh: What It Is and Labneh vs. Greek Yogurt
seo.meta_description: Labneh is yogurt strained until very thick, usually with salt. It shares the same basic principle as Greek yogurt but is often drained further and served as a dip or spread.
seo.search_intent: Understand what labneh is, how removing whey concentrates yogurt, and how it differs in practice from commercial Greek yogurt.

excerpt: Labneh is fermented yogurt concentrated by removing some of its whey. The principle is similar to Greek yogurt, but labneh is usually thicker, salted, and used like a dip or spread with olive oil and za'atar. Exact composition varies substantially among commercial products.
content_html:
Labneh is fermented yogurt that has had some of its whey removed until it becomes thick and spreadable. It is traditional in Lebanon and across the Middle East and is commonly served savory, spread across a plate with olive oil, herbs, or za'atar.

Technically, it belongs to the same broad family of concentrated yogurts as Greek yogurt: water and soluble components are removed after fermentation to create a denser product.

How is labneh made at home?

A basic household version starts with plain yogurt. A small amount of salt is mixed in, the yogurt goes into cloth or a fine filter, and it drains under refrigeration for several hours.

The longer whey drains, the firmer the result. After 8–12 hours it may resemble extremely thick yogurt; longer draining can produce a cream-cheese-like consistency that can even be shaped into balls.

What happens when whey is removed?

As water leaves, protein, fat, minerals, and other solids become more concentrated per 100 g of food. Some lactose and soluble minerals leave with the whey.

A scientific review of yogurt notes that straining can substantially increase protein concentration compared with unstrained yogurt, although the exact result depends on process and formulation.

Labneh and Greek yogurt share the same basic idea

Both are concentrated yogurts. The everyday difference is usually how far the draining goes and how the final food is seasoned and served.

Labneh is often firmer, saltier, and tangier and is treated like a dip or spread. Commercial Greek yogurt is typically sold unsalted with a spoonable texture designed for breakfast, snacks, and recipes.

Commercial labels make the comparison less simple

Not every “Greek-style” product is thickened only by draining; some use milk solids, added proteins, or stabilizers. Industrial labneh can also contain hydrocolloids and vary widely in fat and salt.

A 2024 analysis of labneh sold in the UAE found substantial manufacturer differences in formulation, texture, and nutrition. The name alone does not predict one exact composition.

Does labneh have more protein?

Concentrating yogurt usually increases protein per 100 g because water is removed. But a full-fat labneh and a high-protein Greek yogurt can easily overlap.

If protein is your main reason for choosing, compare grams per 100 g on the actual labels rather than assuming labneh always contains more.

Salt can be an important difference

Many labneh recipes add salt before draining and some commercial products are noticeably salty. Regional nutrition research identifies labneh among fermented dairy foods that can contribute meaningful sodium.

For someone limiting sodium, the label can be more important than comparing fat or protein alone.

How is labneh traditionally served?

It is spread on a plate and finished with olive oil, za'atar, mint, or other herbs. It also works in sandwiches, mezze plates, roasted vegetables, and sauces.

Very dry versions can be rolled into balls and stored in oil in traditional preparations, although homemade labneh should be kept refrigerated and handled hygienically.

Can Greek yogurt be turned into labneh?

Yes. Plain Greek yogurt can be salted and strained longer to create a more concentrated texture. Because it already contains less water, it reaches firmness faster than regular yogurt.

The practical rule: labneh and Greek yogurt are close relatives. Labneh is usually drained further and designed for a savory spreadable use; the specific label determines protein, fat, sodium, and texture.

The exact product can vary across brands and countries, especially in acidity, fat, salt, and moisture. When a recipe depends heavily on one of those properties, the label and actual texture are better guides than assuming every version behaves identically.

faq.question: What is labneh?
faq.answer: It is fermented yogurt strained to remove whey until very thick, usually with some salt.

faq.question: Is labneh the same as Greek yogurt?
faq.answer: They share the same concentration principle, but labneh is usually drained further, saltier, and used as a dip or spread.

faq.question: Can you make labneh from regular yogurt?
faq.answer: Yes. Salted plain yogurt can be drained through cloth in the refrigerator for several hours until it reaches the desired thickness.
